Early signal•Peer-reviewed retrospective development and independent hold-out validation study•September 27, 2026

Local LLM reaches expert-level lecanemab pre-screen accuracy

In a 99-record independent hold-out set, an on-premises language-model pipeline classified lecanemab eligibility with 93.9% accuracy and κ 0.903, outperforming a deterministic rule-based extractor (79.8% accuracy; p=0.0026), but it remains an uncertified single-center retrospective triage tool requiring clinician review.

Key quantitative results: In the 99-record hold-out set, consensus classified 16 as eligible, 43 as potentially eligible and 40 as not eligible. The LLM pipeline achieved 93.9% accuracy (95% CI 88.9% to 98.0%) and κ 0.903 (95% CI 0.810 to 0.968), with six disagreements.

ManagementDisease-modifying treatment eligibility

Added September 28, 2026 · DOI:10.1002/dad2.70495; PMID:42802831

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The privacy-preserving pipeline could reduce chart-review burden and flag missing amyloid, MRI or cognitive data without sending protected health information to an external cloud. Its hold-out performance was comparable to two expert raters, but six errors included medication/disease categorization, context interpretation and threshold application. Prospective multicenter validation is needed before operational deployment.

Study design

The investigators used 97 German memory-clinic consultation reports to optimize prompts, a deterministic comparator and a shared three-class eligibility rule set, then locked the systems before evaluating 99 temporally and patient-wise distinct hold-out reports. Two clinicians independently classified the hold-out set as eligible, potentially eligible or not eligible, with consensus as the reference standard.

Key quantitative results

  • In the 99-record hold-out set, consensus classified 16 as eligible, 43 as potentially eligible and 40 as not eligible. The LLM pipeline achieved 93.9% accuracy (95% CI 88.9% to 98.0%) and κ 0.903 (95% CI 0.810 to 0.968), with six disagreements.
  • For case finding after combining eligible and potentially eligible, sensitivity was 91.5% (95% CI 83.1% to 98.3%) and specificity 97.5% (95% CI 91.1% to 100.0%); PPV was 98%. Eligible-class sensitivity was 100%.
  • The deterministic extractor achieved 79.8% accuracy and κ 0.673. The paired accuracy difference was 14.1 percentage points (95% CI 6.1 to 22.2; McNemar p=0.0026), while individual experts achieved 91.9% and 93.9% accuracy.

What changed

A September 27 publication now provides locked hold-out performance for a locally deployed language model intended to support lecanemab eligibility pre-screening while keeping patient records on premises.

Strength of evidence

Promising but early implementation evidence with strict separation of development and hold-out sets, a consensus reference and paired comparator. Generalizability is limited by retrospective single-center German documentation, only 99 validation records, local AUR-derived rules, missing APOE information and no prospective workflow, patient-safety or access outcome.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The system may help triage charts and identify missing workup elements, but it should not determine eligibility or replace clinician review. Eligibility remains governed by the applicable label, clinical evaluation, amyloid confirmation, MRI findings, comorbidities, concomitant medications and shared decision-making.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to operational scaling of disease-modifying therapy programs, protected-data handling, chart abstraction and consistency of eligibility review. It is management workflow research, not biomarker-validation evidence.

Quanterix or platform relevance

The model extracted eligibility-relevant facts from German narrative memory-clinic reports and fed them to a shared rule-based classifier. Performance depends on local documentation, operationalized criteria and human oversight; the model was not tested as an autonomous decision-maker.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The on-premises design addresses data-protection barriers and may improve screening capacity, but no commercial availability, medical-device authorization, reimbursement or coverage was established.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Was the model tested prospectively in routine care?
No. The study retrospectively classified narrative reports; it did not measure clinician time, missed contraindications in live use, treatment access, safety or patient outcomes.
Why is this not tagged Biomarkers?
Its central question was automated treatment-eligibility triage. Amyloid and MRI information were input variables, not the object of biomarker measurement, validity or interpretation research.
Can the model make treatment decisions?
No. It is an uncertified triage support system, made six hold-out errors and cannot infer facts absent from the record; the authors call for clinician supervision and prospective validation.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Retrospective single-center study using German consultation reports
  • Small 99-record independent validation set with only 16 fully eligible cases
  • Local AUR-derived rules may not match labels or policies in other jurisdictions
  • APOE genotype was missing and source documentation predated routine anti-amyloid implementation
  • Six validation errors included medication, disease, context and threshold interpretation
  • No prospective time-saving, decision-impact, safety, access or patient-outcome evaluation
